identity.title: Powered Industrial Truck Pre-Shift Inspection Log

scan.summary: This is an inspection log for a Toyota 8FGU25 propane forklift, documenting pre-shift safety checks performed in September 2026. The log records pass/fail status for 12 safety-critical components on each inspection date, with operator names and notes. <cite index="2-1,2-2">The requirement cited (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7)) mandates that industrial trucks be examined before being placed in service and shall not be placed in service if the examination shows any condition adversely affecting safety, with such examination made at least daily.</cite>
scan.freshness_note: This log covers September 1–18, 2026, ending just seven days before today (2026-09-25). It is current but represents an incomplete calendar month; the company should be maintaining an active, running log that extends through the current date.

gaps.title: Missing inspection records for September 3–6 and 12–13
gaps.description: The log shows inspections on Sep 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, but the hour meter rises from 4,819 (Sep 2) to 4,834 (Sep 7), proving the truck operated on Sep 3, 4, 5, 6. Similarly, hours rise from 4,866 (Sep 14) to 4,873 (Sep 15), indicating operation on intervening days. No inspections are recorded for these dates. <cite index="8-8,8-9">OSHA 1910.178(q)(7) requires trucks be examined before being placed in service and such examination shall be made at least daily.</cite>
gaps.fix: Obtain the missing inspection records from those dates, or document why the truck was not operated (e.g., weekend, holiday, breakdown). If records are genuinely missing, conduct a retroactive documented review and ensure supervisors confirm equipment safety. Establish a system to flag missing entries immediately.
gaps.locator: page 2, note: 'The hour meter rises between Sep 2 (4,819) and Sep 7 (4,834), which shows the truck ran on the missing days.'
gaps.quote: The hour meter rises between Sep 2 (4,819) and Sep 7 (4,834), which shows the truck ran on the missing days.

gaps.title: Defect on September 9 not resolved before continued operation
gaps.description: On September 9, operator M.C. marked the horn as defective ('X') with the note "Horn not working." <cite index="8-11">OSHA 1910.178(q)(7) requires that defects when found shall be immediately reported and corrected.</cite> The log shows the horn passed inspection ('✓') on September 10 (next day), suggesting the truck may have been operated on September 10 before the defect was confirmed repaired, or the repair was not documented. There is no evidence of when the horn was repaired.
gaps.fix: Document the time the defect was reported, the action taken to repair it, the date/time of repair completion, and verification that the truck was not used between defect discovery and repair completion. This should be added as a note in the defect line or in a separate maintenance log cross-referenced to the inspection log.
gaps.citation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) and 1910.178(p)(4) (conditions requiring removal from service)
gaps.locator: page 1, Sep 9 row and Sep 10 row
gaps.quote: Sep 9: Horn marked 'X' with note 'Horn not working'; Sep 10: Horn marked '✓' with no explanatory note

gaps.title: Supervisor review signature not completed
gaps.description: The log includes a line for "Supervisor review: ____________________ Date: __________" (page 2), but both fields are blank. <cite index="4-4">OSHA guidance indicates that the problem should be recorded on a log and reported to a supervisor immediately.</cite> While federal OSHA does not explicitly mandate written supervisor sign-off on inspection logs, Oregon OSHA or the company's own safety policy may require this. The lack of a supervisor signature means there is no third-party verification that the log has been reviewed or that defects and gaps have been addressed.
gaps.fix: Have a supervisor designated in the Emergency Action Plan sign and date the log monthly (or after the last entry in a period). Include a note of any follow-up actions taken in response to defects or gaps.
gaps.citation: Oregon OSHA may have additional requirements; see company policy

gaps.title: No retention/retention policy stated in the log
gaps.description: The document does not state how long inspection records will be kept. <cite index="8-7">Federal OSHA does not require written records to be retained for a specific period</cite>, but Oregon OSHA or the company's own safety policy may require retention. Without a stated retention policy, there is no assurance that old logs will not be discarded and no audit trail for regulatory inspections.
gaps.fix: Add a header or footer note stating the retention period (e.g., 'Records retained for 3 years' or 'Records retained per Oregon OSHA requirements'). Ensure logs are stored in a secure location accessible to management and regulators.
gaps.citation: Company policy and Oregon OSHA rules (not verified in federal baseline)

The missing inspection dates (Sep 3–6, 12–13) are inferred with high confidence from the hour meter readings, which increase non-linearly. The defect on Sep 9 is explicitly recorded. Moderate confidence: The full implications of the horn defect—whether the truck was used after the defect was found on Sep 9 and before repair verification—cannot be determined from the log alone; this would require checking the separate maintenance records or truck use log, which were not provided. I cannot verify what Oregon OSHA requires beyond the federal baseline (e.g., supervisor sign-off, retention periods, or specific incident reporting). I have not independently checked Oregon OSHA regulations; recommendations on those points are based on common practice. Low confidence: I cannot confirm whether Sep 3–6 and 12–13 were weekends, holidays, or maintenance days—the document does not state this, and the inferred interpretation rests on the assumption that the hour meter is accurate and the truck was not borrowed or transferred.
